findings.claim: The EU is moving toward harmonised maximum vitamin and mineral levels that could force magnesium reformulation, and the 250 mg/day supplemental ceiling is the reference point.
findings.evidence: The Commission will open a public consultation on harmonised Maximum Permitted Levels in Q3 2026, with the final legal act scheduled for Q1 2028; Member States pressed for a formal proposal at the December 2025 Agriculture and Fisheries Council. The method is the 'residual amount' concept — habitual dietary intake subtracted from the Tolerable Upper Intake Level — and experts expect limits to be 'cautious and conservative'. For magnesium the SCF's 2001 UL for supplemental intake is 250 mg/day; Germany's BfR (12 December 2017) recommends no more than 250 mg/day supplemental and advises splitting the dose across at least two intakes per day for tolerability, noting excess causes diarrhoea. text: I read all three sets of findings and synthesized them
below.

I've produced the synthesis above. The short version:

**What
it says together:** The demand-side exc
uses are ruled out — UK confidence is at a two-year high and the category is grow
ing — so the decline points inward, at three st
acked mechanisms: GI tolerability inside b
ottle one, an unmanageable expectation gap (b
ought for sleep, no authorised sleep claim), and an
offer/billing experience that lags a competitor set which
has moved to 60–90 day packs, 20–35
% tiered discounts and non-price retention assets. The EU par
cel duty sits across all of it as a possible step-change cause on the EU side

.

**The honest hole:** almost none of the evidence is br
and-specific, and the retention benchmarks are US-skewed. The find
ings explain why first re
orders are fragile in this category; they do not establish why *your* curve bent,
or when.

summary: Taken together, the three analysts do not produce a single cause — they produce three stacked candidate mechanisms and, importantly, they largely rule out the demand-side excuses. The macro analyst removes "the consumer is broke" (UK confidence at a two-year high in Aug 2026, Major Purchase Index strongest since Dec 2021) and the trends analyst removes "the category is shrinking" (Mintel forecasts 10% value growth; top-five share fell 44%→40%, i.e. you are losing share to challengers, not riding a falling tide). What is left points at three things the brand controls or is exposed to. First, product experience inside bottle one: macro (SCF/BfR — 250 mg/day supplemental UL, mild diarrhoea observed at ~360–365 mg/day, split-dosing advice) and consumer trends (UK HealthUnlocked discontinuation threads on citrate, powders, 400 mg+ doses) converge on GI tolerability as the one mechanism that mechanically produces a visible failure before the reorder date — and the competitors analyst confirms rivals pre-empt exactly this by leading with bisglycinate and explicit "won't upset your stomach" claims. Second, an expectation gap unique to this category in UK/EU: buyers were recruited on a viral sleep promise (H&B — magnesium top search of 2025, glycinate +180%, "sleepy girl mocktail"), but EFSA authorises no sleep claim, so the brand cannot set, manage or defend the expectation that drove order one; combined with form-led shopping (glycinate/threonate/citrate searched by name) this makes defection cheap and rational rather than a loyalty failure. Third, offer and operations at the moment of the second charge: the competitor set has moved to 60–90 day packs (fewer churn decision points), tiered subscription discounts to 20–35%, a published ~22–25p/day price anchor, and non-price retention assets (portals, points, free nutritionist access), while the dominant Trustpilot complaint is silence before billing and cancellations that don't stick — a failure mode the DMCC subscription regime will convert from friction-revenue into explicit churn whenever it commences. Sitting across the EU half of the business is the 1 July 2026 flat €3-per-HS-code duty on low-value parcels, which, if it lands on the customer at the door rather than at checkout, is a textbook order-2 killer and would show up as a step change, not a drift. The critical caveat running through all three sets: almost none of this is brand-specific and much of it is not UK/EU-calibrated (the Recharge 86.6% second-order figure is US-skewed, the TikTok Shop spend data is explicitly US, the search volumes are global). The findings describe a category in which first reorders are structurally fragile; they do not yet tell you why *your* curve bent, or when.

second.claim: Finding 8: commencement is Spring 2027 per the 2 April 2026 DBT consultation response, Taylor Wessing and Reed Smith — with NutraIngredients reporting acceleration to January 2027 — and the finding is rated high confidence. Three different dates (autumn 2026 / Jan 2027 / spring 2027) are in play across the two analysts, and the planning horizon for reminder notices and cancellation rights differs by roughly a year.

first.claim: Finding 1: consumer confidence 'is not the cause' — headline -14 in August 2026, up 11 points year-on-year, Major Purchase Index at its strongest since December 2021. High confidence. (The same analyst's Finding 3 then attributes churn to normalised household cost-cutting via subscription cancellation, and notes the Savings Index fell 5 points — households feel better but are saving less.)

second.claim: Finding 7: UK price sensitivity gives first-order customers a ready-made reason to drop a recurring supplement charge — 40% of VMS users stopped or cut back for financial reasons, 52% of consumers have cut non-essential spend. Note the vintage asymmetry: the macro evidence is August 2026, the trends evidence is 2023 (Mintel) and 2024 (KPMG), so the disagreement may be about time rather than fact — but as presented, one analyst rules affordability out and the other builds a churn mechanism on it.

Reinforced by the competitors analyst's own Finding 3 (a published ~22–25p/day anchor against which premium brands sit 2–4x higher) and Finding 4 (heavy first-order discounting trains buyers to treat full-price order 2 as a price rise).

question: What is the quantified discontinuation rate for magnesium in the first 30–60 days, split by form (bisglycinate vs citrate vs oxide) and by dose (≤250 mg vs 375 mg vs 400 mg+), and does split dosing measurably reduce it?
answer:
No published source gives a 30–60 day discontinuation rate for magnesium split by form and dose — not in trials, not in consumer data. The best available reconstruction from RCTs: (1) GI-attributable discontinuation is small, roughly 0–10% and most commonly ~4%, even above the EU upper level, while diarrhoea *incidence* runs 11–50%; Cochrane 2020 found withdrawal rates on magnesium no different from placebo. (2) The form ranking is not what marketing assumes — in the only well-powered head-to-head at a matched 450 mg elemental dose over 24 weeks, citrate caused MORE GI complaints and more discontinuations (2/46) than oxide (0/46); bisglycinate looks clean at 250 mg but caused the single dropout in a 375 mg crossover and scored worse than microencapsulated oxide on gastric heaviness. (3) Split dosing has NEVER been tested against single dosing for discontinuation or GI symptoms — the rationale is pharmacokinetic (fractional absorption falls from 65% to 11% as dose rises; the unabsorbed remainder is the osmotic driver) and is what the UL re-evaluation authors recommend, but there is no measured effect size.

The 250 vs 375 contradiction is not a disagreement about safety: 250 mg/day is the SCF/EFSA tolerable upper level for supplemental magnesium (osmotic diarrhoea as critical effect, NOAEL 250, UF 1); 375 mg is the EU Nutrient Reference Value, a labelling figure with no safety meaning; the UK EVM set a separate guidance level of 400 mg/day. A 375 mg product sits at 150% of the EU UL while displaying "100% NRV".

Decision implication: the evidence does not support tolerability explaining a LARGE order-2 retention decline — trial GI dropout is single-digit and placebo arms leak nearly as much (10.4% magnesium vs 16.7% placebo withdrew in 4 weeks in the 250 mg bisglycinate trial, mostly unspecified reasons). Reformulating to bisglycinate is the weakest-evidenced of the three options at a 375 mg dose; dose reduction below 250 mg has better mechanistic backing than form-switching, and split dosing is cheap but unevidenced. Most of the trial evidence is US or unstated in origin; the German (Pfaffenrath, Peikert), Dutch (Schutten) and regulatory strands are the genuinely UK/EU-relevant parts.

findings.claim: No RCT or observational study reports magnesium discontinuation rates at 30–60 days split by form and by dose; the closest proxies are trial withdrawal rates and diarrhoea incidence, which are not reported in a form × dose matrix.
findings.evidence: Across every source retrieved — the 2023 UL re-evaluation perspective (which tabulates GI data from Marken 1989, Park 2014, Schutten 2022, Supakatisant 2015, Bashir 1993, Ricci 1991 and three meta-analyses), Cochrane 2020, and four individual trials — no study reports time-to-discontinuation by form and dose. Kass et al. 2012 (22 RCTs, 1173 participants, mean 410 mg/day) found only 3 studies reported diarrhoea-related withdrawals at all.

question: Is there a UK/EU-segmented benchmark for supplement subscription second-order retention (Recharge, Ordergroove, Shopify or Subscrybe data broken out for UK/EU merchants), and has it fallen across 2025–2026?
answer:
No UK/EU-segmented benchmark for supplement subscription second-order retention exists publicly from Recharge, Ordergroove, Shopify, Subbly or Subscrybe — so the question "has the UK/EU baseline fallen across 2025–2026?" cannot be answered from published data, and the flat-vs-falling diagnostic in the brief cannot be run as designed.

Recharge's supplement data (the only vertical-specific first-reorder benchmark that exists: 86.6% of first-time buyers return for a second order, ~1,800 supplement brands, renewal cycles July 2025–June 2026) is explicitly aggregate with no geographic segmentation and no year-over-year comparison — a single 12-month window. Subbly's churn report is the only source that even attempts a country cut ("churn by store's country"), but it publishes no percentages in the text, covers 2024 only, has no year-over-year comparison, and has no supplement breakout. Recharge's flagship Subscription Trend Report 2026 (20,000 brands) carries vertical benchmarks but no regional breakdown. Ordergroove publishes no standalone benchmark report with regional segmentation. The one country-segmented subscription churn dataset found (Statista) is a 2023 Stripe survey of merchant *expectations* of churn, not measured retention, and is paywalled.

The only real time-series signal in the category is global and US-skewed, and it points down: Recharge health & wellness monthly churn moved from ~4.2% (2023, reported in the 2024 State of Subscription Commerce) to 8.8% and "rising" (2026 Subscription Trend Report) — the worst-retaining category on the platform. Two caveats matter. First, it is not UK/EU. Second, it is monthly churn, not order-1→2 conversion; these are different metrics and the supplement curve breaks hardest precisely at the first reorder, so the churn drift does not directly license a claim about second-order retention.

Practical implication: do not let the pack assert that the UK/EU baseline is flat — that is unevidenced in either direction. The directional read from global data mildly favours "the category baseline is also deteriorating," which would push toward the competitive-positioning explanation, but it is not strong enough to rule out brand-level execution. The resolvable path is to request a region-filtered cut (UK/EU supplement first-reorder rate, 2024 vs 2025 vs 2026) from Recharge, which now owns Skio; the underlying data plainly exists and is simply never sliced by geography in public.

## What is happening

Start with the uncomfortable part: none of this research tells you why *your* curve bent, or when. There is no publicly available UK/EU-segmented benchmark for supplement subscription second-order retention from Recharge, Ordergroove, Shopify, Subbly or Subscrybe [c1]. The one vertical-specific number that exists — 86.6% of first-time supplement buyers return for a second order, across ~1,800 brands, renewal cycles July 2025–June 2026 — is aggregate, US-skewed, and has no geographic breakout and no year-over-year comparison [c2]. So you cannot currently tell whether you are tracking a deteriorating category baseline or losing ground on your own.

What is solid: the first reorder is where supplements structurally break. 86.6% versus coffee/tea 99.3%, beauty 97.5%, pet supplies 96.2%, health & wellness 92.9% [c3]. And you are not riding a falling tide — Mintel forecasts 10% UK value growth across 2023–2028, and the top five brands' share of mainstream VMS fell from 44% to 40% in two years as challengers gained [c4]. Nor is the consumer broke: UK confidence hit a two-year high in August 2026 at -14, up 11 points year-on-year, with the Major Purchase Index at its strongest since December 2021 [c5].

The research contradicts itself here and I won't smooth it. The trends analyst builds a churn mechanism on affordability — 40% of VMS users stopped or cut back for financial reasons, 52% of consumers cut non-essential spend [c6]. But that evidence is from 2023 and 2024; the confidence data is August 2026. The disagreement is probably about time, not fact. One real caveat in the recent data: the Savings Index fell 5 points to +22 [c7].

## Most likely causes, ranked

**1. Your offer and the second-charge experience are behind the shelf.** This has the most evidence and the most levers. Competitors default to 60–90 day packs — Bare Biology 180 caps ≈2 months at £34.99, Futuro Labs 180 caps as a 90-day supply at £19.99, DR.VEGAN's cheapest tier 3 pouches every 90 days [c8] — which removes two or three churn decision points a year. Subscription discounts have moved past the 15% norm: DR.VEGAN tiers 15/17.5/20%, Feel runs 23% monthly or 35% on 3-packs [c9]. The strongest players add non-price assets — Feel's health portal, points and tenure gifts; DR.VEGAN free in-house nutritionist consultations; BetterYou's BetterRewards [c10]. Meanwhile the dominant Trustpilot complaint in this set is not price but silence before the charge and cancellations that don't take effect [c11]. Heavy first-order discounting is normal (Feel 50% off month one; BetterYou showing 33–47% off) and trains buyers to read full-price order 2 as a price rise [c12], against a published 22–25p/day anchor that premium brands sit 2–4x above [c13].

**2. An expectation gap you are not allowed to close.** Magnesium topped Holland & Barrett's 2025 searches, with glycinate up 180% on the back of the TikTok "sleepy girl mocktail" [c14]. But EFSA authorises no sleep claim — only muscle and nerve function, psychological function, tiredness and fatigue, energy metabolism and bones [c15]. Buyers now shop by chemical form, searching glycinate, threonate and citrate by name [c16]. You recruited on a promise you may not make, into a market where switching is cheap.

**3. Tolerability — real, but much smaller than the first pass implied.** The follow-up work demotes this. In the only well-powered head-to-head (450 mg elemental, 24 weeks), 4.3% discontinued, and citrate caused more discontinuations (2/46) than oxide (0/46) [c17]. Cochrane found diarrhoea in 11–37% on magnesium versus 10–14% on control, but withdrawal rates no different from placebo [c18]. At 250 mg bisglycinate over 28 days, 10.4% withdrew versus 16.7% on placebo, none GI-attributed [c19]. Bisglycinate is not clean at 375 mg — it caused the only adverse-event dropout in a four-form crossover [c20]. And the 250-vs-375 "contradiction" isn't one: 250 mg is the EU supplemental upper level, 375 mg is a labelling reference value with no safety meaning, and the UK uses a separate 400 mg guidance level [c21]. BfR advises splitting the dose [c22], but split dosing has never been tested against single dosing for GI symptoms or discontinuation [c23].

**4. EU duty — demote to an operational check.** The flat €3 duty per 4-digit tariff heading began 1 July 2026 [c24], but liability sits with the declarant, not the consumer [c25], and a single-SKU supplement order normally attracts one €3 charge [c26]. The ~€2 handling fee was not in force before ~1 November 2026 [c27], and no source reports any dated step change in UK→EU repeat rates in July 2026 [c28]. Whether your customer gets billed depends on your own carrier setup: IOSS covers VAT only, so on duty-unpaid lanes the carrier gates delivery with a payment request [c29]. PPWR packaging obligations from 12 August 2026 confound the same window anyway [c30].

## What this means for positioning

Stop defending a monthly full-price charge and start selling a 60–90 day regimen with a tiered commitment discount. Make the thing you *can* claim — tiredness and fatigue, muscle and nerve function — the spine of the onboarding, and let form (bisglycinate, specified dose, split-dose instruction) carry the differentiation that sleep language legally cannot. Treat pre-billing reminders, one-click cancellation and removable billing details as marketing assets, not compliance chores. DMCC commencement is genuinely disputed across autumn 2026, January 2027 and spring 2027 [c31], but the direction is fixed: reminder notices arrive, and any retention resting on inertia gets reclassified as churn [c32].

## What to test next

1. Ask Recharge (which now owns Skio) for a region-filtered cut: UK/EU supplement first-reorder rate, 2024 vs 2025 vs 2026. The data exists; it is simply never published by geography [c1].
2. Date your own decline. If it is a step change, look at a pricing, pack, shipping or carrier change on that date. If it is a drift, it is competitive.
3. Pull your EU carrier config by destination and check which lanes are duty-unpaid. That is a contract question you can answer today.
4. Run a 90-day pack with a 20%+ tiered discount against your current 30-day, and separately test a pre-billing reminder at T-5 days. Both are cheap and independent.
5. Test split-dose instruction on-pack. Zero evidence it works, near-zero cost.

## What we could not verify

Whether the UK/EU baseline is flat or falling — unevidenced in either direction [c1]. The global signal mildly favours deterioration: health & wellness monthly churn went from ~4.2% in 2023 to 8.8% and rising in 2026 [c33], but monthly churn and order-1→2 conversion are different metrics [c34]. No study anywhere reports magnesium discontinuation at 30–60 days split by form and dose [c35]. And the popular claim that bisglycinate is significantly better tolerated could not be traced to any primary source [c36].

The strongest players add non-price assets — Feel's health portal, points and tenure gifts; DR.VEGAN free in-house nutritionist consultations; BetterYou's BetterRewards [c10]. Meanwhile the dominant Trustpilot complaint in this set is not price but silence before the charge and cancellations that don't take effect [c11]. Heavy first-order discounting is normal (Feel 50% off month one; BetterYou showing 33–47% off) and trains buyers to read full-price order 2 as a price rise [c12], against a published 22–25p/day anchor that premium brands sit 2–4x above [c13].

**2. An expectation gap you are not allowed to close.** Magnesium topped Holland & Barrett's 2025 searches, with glycinate up 180% on the back of the TikTok "sleepy girl mocktail" [c14]. But EFSA authorises no sleep claim — only muscle and nerve function, psychological function, tiredness and fatigue, energy metabolism and bones [c15]. Buyers now shop by chemical form, searching glycinate, threonate and citrate by name [c16]. You recruited on a promise you may not make, into a market where switching is cheap.

**3. Tolerability — real, but much smaller than the first pass implied.** The follow-up work demotes this. In the only well-powered head-to-head (450 mg elemental, 24 weeks), 4.3% discontinued, and citrate caused more discontinuations (2/46) than oxide (0/46) [c17]. Cochrane found diarrhoea in 11–37% on magnesium versus 10–14% on control, but withdrawal rates no different from placebo [c18]. At 250 mg bisglycinate over 28 days, 10.4% withdrew versus 16.7% on placebo, none GI-attributed [c19]. Bisglycinate is not clean at 375 mg — it caused the only adverse-event dropout in a four-form crossover [c20]. And the 250-vs-375 "contradiction" isn't one: 250 mg is the EU supplemental upper level, 375 mg is a labelling reference value with no safety meaning, and the UK uses a separate 400 mg guidance level [c21]. BfR advises splitting the dose [c22], but split dosing has never been tested against single dosing for GI symptoms or discontinuation [c23].

**4. EU duty — demote to an operational check.** The flat €3 duty per 4-digit tariff heading began 1 July 2026 [c24], but liability sits with the declarant, not the consumer [c25], and a single-SKU supplement order normally attracts one €3 charge [c26]. The ~€2 handling fee was not in force before ~1 November 2026 [c27], and no source reports any dated step change in UK→EU repeat rates in July 2026 [c28]. Whether your customer gets billed depends on your own carrier setup: IOSS covers VAT only, so on duty-unpaid lanes the carrier gates delivery with a payment request [c29]. PPWR packaging obligations from 12 August 2026 confound the same window anyway [c30].

## What this means for positioning

Stop defending a monthly full-price charge and start selling a 60–90 day regimen with a tiered commitment discount. Make the thing you *can* claim — tiredness and fatigue, muscle and nerve function — the spine of the onboarding, and let form (bisglycinate, specified dose, split-dose instruction) carry the differentiation that sleep language legally cannot. Treat pre-billing reminders, one-click cancellation and removable billing details as marketing assets, not compliance chores. DMCC commencement is genuinely disputed across autumn 2026, January 2027 and spring 2027 [c31], but the direction is fixed: reminder notices arrive, and any retention resting on inertia gets reclassified as churn [c32].

## What to test next

1. Ask Recharge (which now owns Skio) for a region-filtered cut: UK/EU supplement first-reorder rate, 2024 vs 2025 vs 2026. The data exists; it is simply never published by geography [c1].
2. Date your own decline. If it is a step change, look at a pricing, pack, shipping or carrier change on that date. If it is a drift, it is competitive.
3. Pull your EU carrier config by destination and check which lanes are duty-unpaid. That is a contract question you can answer today.
4. Run a 90-day pack with a 20%+ tiered discount against your current 30-day, and separately test a pre-billing reminder at T-5 days. Both are cheap and independent.
5. Test split-dose instruction on-pack. Zero evidence it works, near-zero cost.

## What we could not verify

Whether the UK/EU baseline is flat or falling — unevidenced in either direction [c1]. The global signal mildly favours deterioration: health & wellness monthly churn went from ~4.2% in 2023 to 8.8% and rising in 2026 [c33], but monthly churn and order-1→2 conversion are different metrics [c34]. No study anywhere reports magnesium discontinuation at 30–60 days split by form and dose [c35]. And the popular claim that bisglycinate is significantly better tolerated could not be traced to any primary source [c36].
